prompt: In a retrieval-augmented generation system over long technical documents, how do chunk size and chunk overlap affect answer quality? How would you choose them?
reference_answer: Chunk size trades retrieval precision against context completeness. Small chunks match queries precisely, but they can split an answer across chunks and lose the surrounding context the LLM needs. Large chunks keep context, but they dilute the embedding (several topics in one vector), lower retrieval precision, and use up the context window and cost. Overlap keeps sentences or ideas that cross chunk boundaries from being cut, at the price of redundant tokens and near-duplicate hits. Choose them empirically: build a small labeled set of questions with known supporting passages, then sweep chunk size (e.g. 256-1024 tokens) and overlap (e.g. 0-20%). Measure retrieval recall@k and answer faithfulness/correctness. Respect document structure (split on headings or sections rather than a fixed character count). Also consider the embedding model's input limit, and parent-document or small-to-big retrieval.
rubric: Explains the precision vs context trade-off of chunk size
Explains what overlap fixes and what it costs
Proposes an empirical way to choose them (labeled questions, retrieval/answer metrics)
answer: Chunk size is a trade-off. Small chunks give precise matches, but an answer can be split across chunks and lose the context the model needs. Big chunks keep context, but the embedding mixes several topics, so retrieval gets less precise, and they fill the context window and cost more. Overlap stops a sentence or idea from being cut at a boundary, but adds duplicate tokens and near-duplicate results. I'd pick them with a small eval: write questions with the passages that answer them, try chunk sizes from about 256 to 1024 tokens and overlaps of 0-20%, and measure recall@k and answer correctness. I'd also split on headings and sections instead of fixed character counts.

prompt: Your tool-using LLM agent for booking meeting rooms sometimes loops: it calls the same search tool again and again with slightly different arguments and never answers. Users wait minutes. What would you investigate, and what would you change?
reference_answer: Investigate with traces: look at the tool calls, tool outputs, and the model's reasoning per step. Common causes: tool results that don't tell the model it succeeded or that nothing was found (empty or ambiguous output), errors swallowed into vague text, a missing stop condition, unclear tool descriptions, or a goal the tools can't satisfy. Fixes: a hard max-step or time budget with a graceful fallback answer; clearer tool descriptions and structured outputs (explicit 'no rooms available for X'); detect repeated identical or near-identical calls and stop or inject a note; let the agent ask the user a clarifying question; add an eval set of such cases and track steps-per-task, success rate, and latency so regressions are caught.
rubric: Uses traces/logs to find the cause (tool outputs, descriptions, stop conditions)
Proposes concrete safeguards (step/time budget, repeat detection, fallback)
Improves tool design or prompts so the model can tell when to stop
Adds measurement (eval cases, steps per task, latency)
answer: First I'd look at traces of the looping runs: each tool call, its output, and what the model did next. Usually the tool output is ambiguous (an empty list without saying 'no rooms free at 3pm'), errors get turned into vague text, or the tool description doesn't say what arguments are valid, so the model keeps retrying. I'd make the tool return structured, explicit results, including a clear 'nothing found'. I'd add a max-step and time budget with a fallback answer, detect repeated near-identical calls and stop or ask the user to clarify, and build eval cases for this pattern that track success rate, steps per task, and latency.

prompt: A fraud classifier reports 99% accuracy on a test set where 1% of transactions are fraud. Is this a good model? Which metrics would you use instead, and why?
reference_answer: Not necessarily. Predicting 'not fraud' for everything also gets 99% accuracy, so accuracy says almost nothing under 1% prevalence. Use metrics focused on the positive class: precision (how many flagged transactions are fraud), recall (how much fraud is caught), F1 or F-beta weighted toward recall if missed fraud is costly, and the precision-recall curve / average precision (more informative than ROC-AUC under heavy imbalance). Pick the decision threshold from the costs of false positives vs false negatives, and check the confusion matrix and calibration.
rubric: Recognizes accuracy is misleading at 1% prevalence (the all-negative baseline)
Names suitable metrics (precision, recall, F1/F-beta, PR-AUC) and what each means
Connects metric/threshold choice to the costs of errors
answer: No. With 1% fraud, predicting 'not fraud' every time already gets 99% accuracy, so this tells us nothing. I'd look at precision (how many flagged are really fraud), recall (how much fraud we catch), F1 or an F-beta that favors recall if missing fraud is expensive, and the precision-recall curve / average precision, which is better than ROC-AUC with heavy imbalance. Then I'd pick the threshold based on the cost of false alarms vs missed fraud, and check the confusion matrix.

prompt: Design the read path of a URL shortener that serves 50,000 redirects per second, with 95% of traffic going to 1% of links. What components would you use and how would you keep latency low?
reference_answer: Redirects are read-heavy and skewed, so cache aggressively. Put a CDN or edge cache in front for the hottest links (cache 301/302 responses with sensible TTLs), then stateless app servers behind a load balancer, then an in-memory cache (Redis/Memcached) holding short-code to URL mappings, then a key-value store (e.g. DynamoDB/Cassandra or sharded Postgres) partitioned by short code as the source of truth. With 95% of traffic on 1% of links, the cache hit rate will be very high. Use read replicas or a replicated KV store for availability. Handle cache misses with request coalescing to avoid stampedes. Keep the analytics write path asynchronous (a queue/stream) so click counting doesn't slow redirects. Monitor p99 latency and cache hit rate.
rubric: Caches hot links (CDN/edge and in-memory cache) and explains why skew helps
Uses a scalable source of truth partitioned by short code with replication
Keeps side work (analytics) off the critical path
Mentions failure/latency concerns (cache misses, stampedes, monitoring)
answer: Reads dominate and are very skewed, so caching is the main tool. A CDN or edge cache serves redirects for the hottest links with a TTL. Behind it, a load balancer and stateless servers check Redis for code to URL. The source of truth is a key-value store like DynamoDB or Cassandra, partitioned by short code and replicated. Since 1% of links get 95% of traffic, the cache hit rate is very high and the DB sees little load. On misses I'd coalesce requests to avoid a stampede on a link that just went viral. Click analytics go to a queue asynchronously so they never slow the redirect. I'd monitor p99 latency and hit rate.

prompt: You train a model to predict galaxy redshifts from broadband photometry, using a spectroscopic training sample. Why might it perform worse on the full photometric survey than on your test split, and how would you detect and reduce that?
reference_answer: The spectroscopic sample is not representative: it is brighter, lower redshift, and biased toward certain galaxy types because spectroscopic targeting and success depend on magnitude and color. So the survey is a covariate-shifted (and partly out-of-distribution) population, and a random test split from the spec sample hides this. Detect it by comparing feature distributions (color-magnitude space), using held-out deeper or fainter spec fields, examining the outlier fraction and bias vs magnitude, and checking calibration of the predicted redshift PDFs. Reduce it with reweighting (e.g. nearest-neighbor or density-ratio weights) to match the photometric distribution, augmenting with deeper or more representative spectroscopy or many-band data, flagging out-of-coverage objects, and providing uncertainty estimates (PDFs) instead of point estimates.
rubric: Identifies the non-representative spectroscopic training sample (covariate shift)
Explains how to detect it beyond a random test split
Proposes mitigation (reweighting, representative data, flagging, uncertainty)
answer: The spectroscopic training set isn't representative of the survey. Spectroscopy targets brighter, lower-redshift galaxies and some types more than others, so the full photometric sample has a different color-magnitude distribution, and parts of it have no training coverage. A random test split from the spec sample hides this. I'd compare feature distributions, test on deeper spec fields, and look at bias and outlier fraction vs magnitude and the calibration of the redshift PDFs. To reduce it: reweight the training set to match the photometric distribution (nearest-neighbor weights), add more representative spectroscopy or many-band data, flag objects outside the training coverage, and output PDFs with uncertainties.
